History & Physical (Detailed)

Consult Summary:
40-year-old woman with childhood asthma presents via video visit with 2-day history of progressive wheeze and shortness of breath after heavy dust exposure; clinician advised in-person assessment to rule out asthma exacerbation versus allergic reaction.

History:
• Presenting complaint – Wheeze and shortness of breath.  
• Onset – Began ~2 days ago, about one hour after cleaning dusty carpet.  
• Course – Gradually worsening; notably worse at night; today causing difficulty completing sentences.  
• Associated symptoms – No chest pain on deep inspiration, no dizziness/light-headedness.  
• Hydration – Drinking 4–5 glasses of water/day.  
• Exposures – Heavy dust during house cleaning; possible dust allergy.  
• Self-care to date – Has not taken any medication for current episode; owns an old asthma inhaler but has not used it.

Past Medical History:
• Asthma in childhood; occasional exertional wheeze as adult; previously required oral steroids.  
• Seasonal allergic rhinitis/hay fever in summer.  
• No other chronic illnesses mentioned.

Medications:
• Asthma inhaler (type and dose/route/frequency not documented); last obtained “a couple of months ago.”  
• No regular antihistamine; none currently in home.  
Allergies: Denies known drug or other allergies.

Social History:
• Location: At home; GP surgery “minutes’ drive away.”  
• Smoking, alcohol, occupation, and substance use – Not discussed (missing).

Family History:
• Not discussed.

Physical Examination:
Vitals – Not recorded (video consultation).  
General / Chest exam – Not performed or documented.  
Other systems – Not examined.

Investigations:
• None performed during call.  
• Planned: Pulse oximetry and additional in-clinic tests (e.g., peak-flow/spirometry per clinician statement).

Assessment & Plan:
Overall Impression:
Likely acute asthma exacerbation triggered by dust exposure; allergic bronchospasm also considered.

DDx Integration (consistent with transcript):
1. Asthma exacerbation – Supported by childhood asthma history, wheeze after dust exposure, nocturnal worsening; no infection signs.  
2. Dust-mite/allergic bronchospasm – Supported by hay-fever history and trigger; persistence >48 h argues for concomitant asthma.  
(PE, infection, COPD low likelihood; no conflicting data).

Issue 1 – Acute wheeze/shortness of breath  
• Assessment: Probable asthma flare vs allergic reaction.  
• Plan:  
  – Attend GP/urgent care today for objective assessment (pulse oximetry, peak flow, chest exam).  
  – Obtain and take OTC non-sedating antihistamine en route if available.  
  – Bring existing inhaler; use as directed by GP if airflow obstruction confirmed.  
  – GP to consider short course of oral steroids if moderate/severe obstruction.  
  – Safety-net: Call emergency services if worsening breathlessness, inability to speak in full sentences, chest tightness, or faintness.

Issue 2 – Asthma (chronic)  
• Assessment: Sub-optimally controlled; no regular follow-up.  
• Plan:  
  – Post-acute review of asthma control and inhaler technique.  
  – Update prescriptions (SABA, possible inhaled corticosteroid).  
  – Provide written asthma action plan.

Issue 3 – Allergic rhinitis/hay fever  
• Assessment: Intermittent seasonal; may contribute to airway hyper-reactivity.  
• Plan:  
  – Initiate regular/non-sedating antihistamine during high-pollen seasons.  
  – Discuss environmental controls and as-needed intranasal steroid at follow-up.

General plan items:  
• Letter to GP summarizing telehealth encounter to facilitate prompt in-person review.  
• Follow-up through app after GP visit or sooner if symptoms escalate.

Quality checks:
● Missing elements – No vitals or physical exam; medication reconciliation (complete list) not obtained; smoking/alcohol history not documented.  
● No explicit conflicts between transcript and DDx.  
● Transcript quality acceptable; brief loss of video noted but audio adequate.
